title: Review: Chemistry — Chemical reactions
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for KS3 Science (chemistry) (status of the source: authored-reviewed-reverified-2026-10-08). Terms and clues: C4#c18 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; C4.3#xt2 term and clue written for the game; C4#c21 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; C4#c10 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: C4#x11 (written for the game), C4#q16, C4#x13 (written for the game), C4#q17, C4#x12 (written for the game), C4#x18 (written for the game), C4#q14, C4#q15, C4#q12, C4#x19 (written for the game), C4#q10, C4#x20 (written for the game). The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Oxide
items.clue: A compound of an element joined with oxygen

items.label: Litmus
items.clue: Red in one kind of solution and blue in the opposite kind.

items.label: Fuel
items.clue: A substance that is burned to transfer energy, such as methane, butane, petrol or wax.

questions.stem: Wood, petrol and methane are all fuels. What happens when any fuel burns?

options.text: It is destroyed and turned into energy
It melts and evaporates away as a gas
It reacts with oxygen and gives out energy
It breaks down with heat, needing no oxygen

questions.explanation: Combustion is a reaction of a fuel with oxygen that transfers energy to the surroundings.

questions.stem: A substance dissolves in water. Which result shows that the substance is an alkali?

options.text: It neutralises acids
It turns blue litmus red
It has a pH below 7
It reacts with nothing

questions.explanation: Yes. A substance that dissolves in water and neutralises acids is a base that dissolves: an alkali. Its solution also has a pH above 7.

questions.stem: Burning magnesium and rusting iron are both oxidation reactions. What happens in both?

options.text: The metal joins with oxygen
The metal gives off oxygen gas
The metal burns with a flame
The metal loses some of its mass

questions.explanation: In oxidation a substance gains oxygen: both metals join with oxygen to form metal oxides.

questions.stem: When an alkali neutralises an acid, what happens to the acid?

options.text: It breaks down on its own and stops being acid
It reacts with the alkali to make a salt
It is simply stopped from burning anything
It is only diluted by the water in the alkali

questions.explanation: Yes. Neutralisation is a reaction between the acid and the alkali. It makes a salt and water.

questions.stem: Copper is less reactive than magnesium. A piece of copper is put into magnesium sulfate solution. What happens?

options.text: Copper displaces magnesium, which coats it
Magnesium displaces copper from the solution
Nothing: copper cannot displace magnesium
Copper dissolves, turning the solution blue

questions.explanation: Only a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its compound, so there is no reaction.

options.text: A soft metal that reacts with water
A soluble base that neutralises acids
A neutral liquid with a pH of 7
A harmless liquid that waters acids down

questions.explanation: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water; it neutralises acids.

questions.stem: Iron is more reactive than copper. An iron nail is left in blue copper sulfate solution. A brown coating forms. What is it?

options.text: Iron that has changed into copper
Rust, because the iron nail is wet
Copper, pushed out of the copper sulfate
Copper sulfate that has stuck to the nail

questions.explanation: Yes. This is displacement: the more reactive iron takes copper's place, making iron sulfate and copper. The copper forms the coating.

questions.stem: Which statement is true of every acid?

options.text: It eats away any material it touches
It can be neutralised by an alkali
It has the same pH as all other acids
It bubbles and fizzes on its own

questions.explanation: Yes. Every acid reacts with an alkali and is neutralised, making a salt and water. That is how acids and alkalis are defined.

questions.stem: Copper is heated in a hot, blue Bunsen flame. Its surface turns black. What is the black layer?

options.text: Copper oxide, as oxygen joined the copper
Soot (carbon) left on it by the flame
Copper changed by heat, with nothing added
Copper that has turned into carbon

questions.explanation: Yes. Copper reacts with oxygen from the air to make black copper oxide. Gaining oxygen like this is oxidation.

questions.stem: Alkali is added to an acid a little at a time, until far more has been added than is needed to neutralise it. What is the mixture now?

options.text: Neutral, as the acid has been cancelled out
Acidic, as it started off as an acid
Alkaline, as there is alkali left over
Both strongly acidic and strongly alkaline

questions.explanation: Once all the acid has reacted, any extra alkali stays in the mixture and makes it alkaline.

questions.stem: Magnesium burns in air with a bright white flame. Which substance is made?

options.text: Soot made of carbon
Carbon dioxide and water
Nothing: it burns away
Solid magnesium oxide

questions.explanation: Yes. A metal burns by joining with oxygen to make its oxide: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide, a white powder.

questions.stem: Which pair of substances would react together in a neutralisation reaction?

options.text: Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide
Hydrochloric acid and sulfuric acid
Sodium hydroxide and distilled water
Hydrochloric acid and magnesium metal

questions.explanation: Neutralisation needs an acid and a base: hydrochloric acid is an acid, sodium hydroxide an alkali.
